questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy has a valid Klonopin prescription for 60 tablets that was issued two weeks ago. Only 20 tablets are in stock, and the patient asks to receive 20 now and the balance later. Under federal law, which approach is permissible?

choices.text: Dispense 20 now, but require a new prescription before dispensing any remaining tablets.
Dispense 20 now; record each partial fill, keep the aggregate at 60 or less, and finish within six months of issue.
Dispense 20 now and restart the six-month dispensing window when the balance is received.
Refuse the partial fill because Schedule IV prescriptions must be dispensed in a single transaction.
Dispense the balance later without documenting each partial because the original order already states 60 tablets.

questions.stem: A Halcion e-prescription was issued two months ago for 30 tablets with one refill, and that refill has been used. The prescriber now telephones the pharmacist and authorizes two additional refills of 30 tablets each. What is the correct federal handling?

choices.text: Require a new prescription because Schedule IV refill authorization can never be added after issuance.
Add the refills and start a new six-month dispensing period on the date of the telephone call.
Add them and record the date, refill quantity, number added, and receiver of the oral authorization in the electronic record.
Add them only if each refill is reduced below the original 30-tablet quantity.
Treat the telephone authorization as an emergency oral prescription under the Schedule II procedure.

questions.stem: A patient requests a permissible transfer of an unfilled electronic Sonata prescription that includes two authorized refills to another DEA-registered retail pharmacy. The sending pharmacist asks whether only the initial fill can move while the two refills remain at the original pharmacy. What is the correct federal result?

choices.text: Only the initial fill transfers; the authorized refills must remain at the original pharmacy.
The initial fill transfers now, and each authorized refill may later be transferred separately.
The authorized refills transfer with the original prescription, so the entire prescription moves to the receiving pharmacy.
The receiving pharmacy must cancel both refills because controlled-substance refills cannot transfer electronically.
The patient may divide the refills between both pharmacies if the two pharmacists agree.
